Phocas alienated Persian King Chosroes through suspicious executions, which promptly triggered a devastating eastern invasion. [PDF p. 155] Persian armies rapidly occupied Syria and eventually reached the Asian shore opposite Constantinople. [PDF p. 155] African exarch Heraclius successfully overthrew the tyrant and assumed the imperial throne in 610. [PDF p. 156] Heraclius inherited a treasuryless empire plagued by multiple foreign invasions. [PDF p. 156] He secured Church loans and reorganized military forces to counter the Persian threat. [PDF p. 158] His strategic campaigns between 622 and 627 successfully cleared Asia Minor of enemy forces. [PDF p. 161] Heraclius penetrated deep into Media, which forced Chosroes to abandon his western conquests. [PDF p. 162] A coordinated Avar and Persian siege of Constantinople ultimately failed due to naval defense. [PDF p. 163] Heraclius delivered a decisive blow at Nineveh, which led to Chosroes's murder. [PDF p. 164] The 628 peace treaty restored all occupied territories and the sacred True Cross. [PDF p. 164]

This magnificent victory occurred precisely as Arab forces began their relentless territorial expansion. [PDF p. 165] Both empires were completely exhausted by their prolonged mutual warfare. [PDF p. 184] Heraclius faced simultaneous revolts and a sudden Saracen invasion that rapidly consumed the Syrian provinces. [PDF p. 187] Roman defeats at Ajnadin and the eventual fall of Jerusalem marked a catastrophic turning point. [PDF p. 188] Heraclius died in 641 while his remaining provinces crumbled under continuous Arab military pressure. [PDF p. 189] Social transformation occurred extensively from the reign of Constantine to Heraclius. [PDF p. 167] Latin gradually vanished from administration as Christian moral reforms abolished gladiatorial games and infant exposure. [PDF p. 168] Monasticism expanded rapidly, though the author explicitly critiques its withdrawal from civic responsibilities. [PDF p. 173] He defends Byzantine society against modern accusations of universal cowardice and moral decay. [PDF p. 177]

Constantine IV subsequently preserved the empire by successfully resisting a massive Arab siege of Constantinople. [PDF p. 170] The strategic deployment of Greek fire secured a crucial naval victory that ended the immediate threat. [PDF p. 170] The empire also reorganized its provincial administration into a standardized military theme system. [PDF p. 167] Constantine IV later accommodated the Bulgarian settlement in the Balkan peninsula. [PDF p. 171] The author details the Sixth Council, which condemned Monothelite Christological doctrines. [PDF p. 171] Following this period of stabilization, Justinian II ascended the throne as an intensely autocratic ruler. [PDF p. 172] His reckless wars and brutal financial exactions generated profound resentment across military and civilian ranks. [PDF p. 173]

The supplied material ends abruptly during Justinian II's early reign, leaving subsequent rebellions undocumented. [PDF p. 174] The author relies heavily on later chroniclers for certain Arab campaign details, which limits immediate contemporary verification. [PDF p. 160] Uncertainties regarding the precise chronology of some Bulgarian migrations remain partially unresolved. [PDF p. 171]
